parsed.title: Simulation and Synthesized Data in Training and Evaluating Driving Policies
outline: Introduction to End-to-End Neural Network Approaches
Mid-Level Representations and Recurrent Neural Networks
Role of CARLA Simulator in Autonomous Driving Research
parsed.markdown: End-to-end neural network models have been widely applied to autonomous driving, where convolutional neural networks (CNNs) learn to generate steering commands directly from front-facing camera images, trained on diverse driving data including video and steering inputs [1]. ChauffeurNet advances this approach by utilizing mid-level input representations combined with recurrent neural networks (RNNs) to output driving trajectories, enabling training on both real and simulated data and supporting closed-loop simulation testing before real-world deployment [2]. The CARLA simulator serves as a comprehensive open-source platform that facilitates development, training, and validation of autonomous driving models by providing flexible sensor and environment configurations along with digital urban assets, supporting evaluation of various driving approaches including end-to-end learning and reinforcement learning [3]. Despite these advances, pure imitation learning methods face significant limitations such as error accumulation and distribution shift during closed-loop operation, leading to failures like getting stuck or collisions even with large datasets and mid-level representations [1, 2]. Although models like ChauffeurNet and simulators like CARLA enable closed-loop testing, there remains a critical gap in effectively mitigating these issues, indicating the need for novel methods to improve robustness and reliability in autonomous driving policies trained with simulation and synthesized data [2, 3].
